source_text: Operae pretium est cognoscere illorum pietatem, ut ex ns quae clementer ac pie faciunt possit intellegi, qualia sint quae ab iis contra iura pietatis geruntur. ac ne quem uidear inclementer incessere, aliquam mihi personam poeticam sumam, quae sit uel maximum pietatis exemplum. aput Maronem rex ille, quo iustior alter nec pietate fuit nec bello maior et armis, quae nobis documenta iustitiae protulit? uinxerat et post terga manus, quos mitteret umbris inferias, caeso sparsurus sanguine flammas. quid potest hac pietate ... clementius, quam mortuis humanas uictimas immolare et ignem cruore hominum tamquam oleo pascere? sed fortasse hoc non ipsius uitium fuerit, sed : poetae, qui insignem pietate uirum insigni scelere foedauerit. ubi est igitur, o poeta, pietas illa quam saepissime laudas? ecce pius Aeneas Sulmone creatos quattuor hic iuuenes, totidem quos educat Ufens, uiuentis rapit, inferias quos immolet umbris captiuoque rogi perfundat sanguine flammas. cur ergo dicebat eodem ipso tempore quo uinctos homines ad immolationem mittebat: equidem et uiuis concedere uellem, cum uiuos quos habebat in potestate uice pecudum iuberet occidi? sed haec, ut dixi, culpa non illius fuit, qui litteras fortasse non didicerat, sed tua: qui cum esses eruditus, ignorasti tamen quid esset pietas, et illut ipsum quod nefarie, quod detestabiliter fecit, pietatis esse officium credidisti; uidelicet ob hoc unum pius uocatur, quod patrem dilexit. quid quod bonus Aeneas haut aspernanda precantis trucidauit? adiuratus enim per eundem patrem et spes surgentis Iuli, nequaquam pepercit furiis accensus et ira. quisquamne igitur hunc putet aliquid in se uirtutis habuisse, qui et furore tamquam stipula exarserit et manium patris per quem rogabatur oblitus iram frenare non quiuerit? nullo igitur modo pius, qui non tantum non repugnantes, sed etiam precantes interemit. dicet hic aliquis: quae ergo aut ubi aut qualis est pietas?* nimirum aput eos qui bella nesciunt, qui concordiam cum omnibus seruant, qui amici sunt etiam inimicis, qui omnes homines pro fratribus diligunt, qui cohibere iram sciunt omnemque animi furorem tranquilla moderatione lenire. quanta igitur caligo, quanta tenebrarum et errorum nubes hominum pectora obduxit, qui cum se maxime pios putant, tum maxime fiunt inpii? quanto enim religiosius terrenis istis simulacris inseruiunt, tanto magis scelerati aduersus nomen uerae diuinitatis exsistunt. itaque pro merito inpietatis suae grauioribus malis saepe negantur: quorum causam quia nesciunt, fortunae culpa omnis adscribitur, et locum inuenit Epicuri philosophia nihil ad deos pertinere censentis nec gratia eos tangi nec ira moueri, quia et contemptores eorum saepe uideant beatos et cultores saepe miseros. quod eo nt quia cum religiosi uideantur et natura boni, nihil tale creduntur mereri quale saepe patiuntur. consolantur se tamen accusatione fortunae nec sentiunt quod si esset ulla, cultoribus suis numquam noceret. merito igitur huiusmodi pietatem poena consequitur et offensa diuinitas scelere hominum praue religiosorum graui eos infortunio mactat: qui licet sanctis moribus uiuant in summa fide atque innocentia, tamen quia deos colunt, quorum ritus inpios ac profanos deus uerus odio habet, a iustitia et a nomine uerae pietatis alieni sunt. nec est difficile docere cur deorum cultores boni et iusti esse non possint. quomodo enim sanguine abstinebunt qui colunt cruentos deos Martem atque Bellonam? quomodo aut parentibus parcent qui expulsorem patris sui Iouem aut natis ex se infantibus qui Saturnum? quomodo pudicitiam tuebuntur qui colunt deam nudam et adulteram et quasi aput deos prostitutam? quomodo se rapinis et fraudibus abstinebunt qui Mercuri furta nouerunt docentis non fraudis esse decipere, sed astutiae? quomodo libidines cohercebunt qui Iouem Herculem Liberum Apollinem ceterosque uenerantur, quorum adulteria et stupra in mares et feminas non tantum doctis nota sunt, sed exprimuntur etiam in theatris atque cantantur, ut sint omnibus notiora? possuntne inter haec iusti esse hommes, qui etiamsi natura sint boni, ab ipsis tamen diis erudiantur ad iniustitiam? ad placandum enim deum quem colas iis rebus opus est, quibus illum gaudere ac delectari scias. sic fit ut uitam colentium deus pro qualitate numinis sui formet, quoniam religiosissimus est cultus imitari.
pass_a_gloss: Pagan 'piety' sacrifices captives to the dead and feeds fire with human blood — no piety at all. True piety is with those who keep peace, love even enemies as brothers, and calm rage. The more religiously they serve earthly images, the more wicked they are against the true God; those who imitate bloody, adulterous gods cannot be just, for the most religious worship is to imitate the god you serve.
pass_b_english: It is worth knowing their piety, that from the things they do mildly and piously it may be understood what sort of things are done by them against the rights of piety. And lest I seem to attack anyone harshly, I will take for myself some poetic person who is the greatest example of piety. In Maro that king than whom none was more just in piety nor greater in war and arms — what proofs of justice did he put forward for us? He had bound behind their backs the hands of those he would send as offerings to the shades, about to sprinkle the flames with slaughtered blood. What can be milder than this piety … than to sacrifice human victims to the dead and to feed the fire with the blood of humans as with oil? But perhaps this was not his own fault, but the poet's, who stained a man outstanding in piety with an outstanding crime. Where then, O poet, is that piety which you praise so often? See: pious Aeneas seizes four youths born at Sulmo, and as many as Ufens raises, living, to sacrifice them as offerings to the shades and to pour captive blood over the flames of the pyre. Why then was he saying at the very time when he was sending bound humans to immolation, 'I would indeed wish to spare the living also,' when he ordered those living whom he held in his power to be killed in place of cattle? But this, as I said, was not that man's fault, who perhaps had not learned letters, but yours: who, though you were learned, still did not know what piety is, and believed that very thing which he did wickedly and detestably to be the duty of piety; namely he is called pious for this one thing, that he loved his father. What of the fact that good Aeneas slaughtered one praying for things not to be scorned? For though adjured by the same father and the hopes of rising Iulus, he by no means spared, inflamed with furies and anger. Would anyone then think this man had any virtue in himself, who both blazed with fury as with stubble and, forgetful of his father's shades by whom he was asked, could not rein in anger? In no way then pious, who killed not only those not resisting but even those praying.

Someone will say here: what then, or where, or of what sort is piety? Surely with those who do not know wars, who keep concord with all, who are friends even to enemies, who love all humans as brothers, who know how to check anger and to soften every fury of the mind with calm moderation. How great then the darkness, how great the cloud of shadows and errors that has covered human breasts, who when they think themselves most pious then become most impious? For the more religiously they serve these earthly images, the more criminal they stand against the name of true divinity. And so for the merit of their impiety they are often denied by heavier evils: whose cause, because they do not know it, is all ascribed to the fault of fortune, and Epicurus's philosophy finds a place, judging that nothing pertains to the gods and that they are touched neither by favor nor moved by anger, because they often see both their despisers blessed and their worshipers wretched. Which happens because when they seem religious and good by nature, they are believed to deserve nothing such as they often suffer. Yet they console themselves by accusing fortune and do not sense that if there were any, it would never harm its worshipers. Deservedly therefore punishment follows this sort of piety, and offended divinity by the crime of humans wrongly religious slaughters them with heavy misfortune: who though they live with holy manners in highest faith and innocence, yet because they worship gods whose impious and profane rites the true God holds in hatred, are alien from justice and from the name of true piety.

Nor is it hard to teach why worshipers of the gods cannot be good and just. For how will they abstain from blood who worship the bloody gods Mars and Bellona? How will they spare parents who worship Jupiter the expeller of his father, or infants born from themselves who worship Saturn? How will they guard chastity who worship a naked and adulterous goddess and as it were prostituted among the gods? How will they abstain from robberies and frauds who have known the thefts of Mercury teaching that to deceive is not fraud but cleverness? How will they check lusts who venerate Jupiter, Hercules, Liber, Apollo and the rest, whose adulteries and shames against males and females are known not only to the learned but are even expressed in theaters and sung, that they may be more known to all? Can humans be just amid these things, who even if they are good by nature are nevertheless trained to injustice by the gods themselves? For to placate the god you worship you need those things by which you know him to rejoice and be delighted. So it happens that the god shapes the life of the worshipers according to the quality of his own divinity, since the most religious worship is to imitate.
